The Central Bank of Nigeria has introduced a minimum paid-up capital requirement of N15bn for companies issuing foreign currency-backed stablecoins, including those pegged to the United States dollar, as part of new regulations governing virtual assets and digital payment services in Nigeria. The requirement is contained in the Regulations for the Operations of Non-Security Virtual Assets in Nigeria, released by the apex bank on Friday, following a circular dated 5 November, 2026, and signed by the Director of the Payments System Policy Department, Musa Jimoh. Under Section 15.2 of the regulations, the CBN stated, “A Class 2 Licensed Issuer shall maintain minimum paid-up capital of fifteen billion Naira (N15,000,000,000), or such higher amount as the Bank may prescribe, on entry and at all times thereafter.” The provision applies to Class 2 stablecoins, which are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value against foreign currencies, including the US dollar. The regulations also prescribe a lower capital threshold of N10bn for issuers of naira-referenced stablecoins, classified as Class 1, while companies providing other non-security virtual asset services must maintain at least N1bn in paid-up capital. The CBN stated, “A Class 1 Licensed Issuer shall maintain paid-up capital of ten billion Naira (N10,000,000,000), or such higher amount as the Bank may prescribe, on entry and at all times thereafter.” For other virtual asset service providers, the regulations specify that the N1bn requirement must be maintained separately from capital committed to licences issued by the Securities and Exchange Commission or other regulatory authorities. The new framework establishes different capital requirements for stablecoin issuers and other service providers, reflecting the varying financial and operational risks associated with their activities. According to the document, “Capital shall be separate from and additional to issuer reserves, the CBN reserve deposit, customer funds and assets and operational liquidity.” This means operators cannot use the same funds to satisfy multiple regulatory obligations, including capital adequacy and reserves backing stablecoins already in circulation. The regulations further require eligible capital to be held as cash in designated accounts with the CBN or in approved Federal Government securities subject to the bank’s control. Operators whose capital falls below the prescribed minimum must notify the CBN immediately and submit a restoration plan within 10 business days. The regulator may restrict new token issuance or customer onboarding until compliance is restored. Beyond capital requirements, the CBN introduced strict rules on the assets backing stablecoins, requiring issuers to maintain reserves equivalent to at least 100 per cent of outstanding obligations, alongside an additional two per cent buffer against potential losses. It stated, “No Licensed Issuer shall issue new stablecoin tokens (mint) unless, at the time of minting, equivalent Eligible Reserve Assets have been received and held in the Reserve Pool.” Stablecoin holders must also be allowed to redeem their tokens at face value, generally no later than the next business day after a valid request, without charges for standard redemptions. The regulations prohibit algorithmic stablecoins that rely primarily on supply adjustments rather than adequate reserve assets, alongside tokens linked to fiat currencies but backed mainly by other cryptocurrencies. The CBN also established additional supervisory requirements for stablecoins whose circulating value exceeds N500bn for 30 consecutive days or which are used by more than five million people in Nigeria. Such instruments will be classified as systemically important, attracting enhanced regulatory scrutiny. The framework further covers cryptocurrency exchanges, digital wallets, payment gateways, remittances, custody services and platform-facilitated peer-to-peer transactions. It introduces obligations relating to anti-money laundering, terrorist financing, customer identification, transaction monitoring, cybersecurity, consumer protection and regulatory reporting. The rules apply to both domestic and foreign operators offering regulated services to Nigerians, regardless of whether they maintain a physical office in the country. However, the CBN clarified that securities-related virtual assets would remain under the SEC’s jurisdiction, with both regulators coordinating where their responsibilities overlap.
